title: Title 10 and Title 50
section: The legal hinge: the definition of covert action
text:
The legal hinge: the definition of covert action
The line is drawn by one definition, added to the National Security Act in 1991 and now at 50 U.S.C. 3093(e). Covert action is activity to influence political, economic, or military conditions abroad where the U.S. role is intended not to be apparent or acknowledged. Covert action needs a written presidential finding and notice to the intelligence committees under the rules described on the Intelligence Oversight Act page.
The definition then excludes four categories. The one that matters here is “traditional diplomatic or military activities.” Anything that qualifies as a traditional military activity is not covert action, needs no finding, and is overseen by the armed services committees instead.
The statute does not define traditional military activities. The 1991 conference report described them as activities by military personnel under the direction and control of a U.S. military commander, before or during hostilities that are ongoing or anticipated, where the U.S. role in the overall operation is apparent or will be acknowledged. How far “anticipated” hostilities and “overall operation” stretch is the core of the dispute.
Two terms are often confused. A clandestine operation hides the operation itself. A covert operation hides who is behind it. Military special operations are routinely clandestine without being covert in the statutory sense.

title: Title 10 and Title 50
text:
Where the line is contested
Special operations outside war zones. Military preparation of the environment, such as reconnaissance and building local networks, can look identical to intelligence collection. Programs under Section 127e fund surrogate forces for counterterrorism and report to the armed services committees.
Cyber operations. Whether offensive cyber operations against an adversary’s networks in peacetime required a finding was argued for years. Section 394 answered it in 2018 by declaring clandestine military cyber activity a traditional military activity.
Mixed operations. The 2011 raid that killed Osama bin Laden was carried out by military personnel but, by official accounts, conducted under CIA authority. It is the standard illustration that the title describes the authority and chain of command for a mission, not the uniform worn by the people doing it.
Dual roles. One officer has served as both director of the National Security Agency and commander of U.S. Cyber Command, sitting in both systems at once.

title: Title 10 and Title 50
section: Why the distinction matters for oversight
text:
Why the distinction matters for oversight
The two committee systems see different things. Covert action comes with a statutory finding and prior notice. Military operations historically came with fewer formal notice rules, on the theory that they are acknowledged and run through an accountable chain of command.
Critics argue this creates an incentive to label sensitive activity as military in order to avoid the finding process. Defenders reply that military operations are subject to the law of armed conflict, the chain of command, and the Uniform Code of Military Justice, and that the intelligence framework was never meant to cover them.
Congress has responded by adding notice rules on the Title 10 side, one activity at a time: sensitive military operations (10 U.S.C. 130f), sensitive military cyber operations (10 U.S.C. 395), and special operations support programs. Most of these arrived through the annual defense authorization. The result is a patchwork that narrows the gap without merging the two systems.

title: Title 10 and Title 50
text:
Neighboring titles
The same kind of question, which title and therefore whose rules, comes up elsewhere in this wiki:

Title 10 and Title 22. Training and equipping foreign forces can be done by the Defense Department under Chapter 16 of Title 10 or by the State Department under the Foreign Assistance Act and Arms Export Control Act. The choice determines who decides, who pays, and which committees oversee it.
Title 10 and Title 32. National Guard members can serve under federal command or under their governor with federal funding. As the mobilization authorities page explains, the status decides whether the Posse Comitatus Act applies.
Title 50 and Title 18. Intelligence collection under FISA and criminal investigation run on different standards, and the wall between them has been raised and lowered several times.

title: Title 10 and Title 50
text:
Limits of this page
This is an orientation to a debate, written as a neutral summary. The meaning of traditional military activities rests on legislative history and executive branch practice, much of it classified, so published accounts differ. Check the linked statute pages and primary sources before relying on a specific claim.

title: War Powers Resolution
text:
In force Pub. L. 93-148 87 Stat. 555 50 U.S.C. 1541-1550
Passed over President Nixon’s veto, the War Powers Resolution is Congress’s framework statute for sharing the decision to commit U.S. forces to hostilities. It requires consultation before forces are introduced, a report to Congress within 48 hours, and withdrawal within 60 days (plus a 30-day drawdown) unless Congress declares war or passes a specific authorization.

title: War Powers Resolution
text:
Key provisions

Sec. 2(c): states that the President may introduce forces into hostilities only under a declaration of war, specific statutory authorization, or a national emergency created by an attack on the United States.
Sec. 3: consultation with Congress ‘in every possible instance’ before introducing forces.
Sec. 4(a)(1): written report within 48 hours of introducing forces into hostilities or imminent hostilities.
Sec. 5(b): the 60-day termination clock, extendable by 30 days for safe withdrawal.
Sec. 5(c): withdrawal by concurrent resolution, widely viewed as unenforceable after INS v. Chadha (1983); expedited joint-resolution procedures were added in 1983.
Sec. 8: authority to use force may not be inferred from appropriations acts or treaties.

title: War Powers Resolution
text:
Why it matters
It is the reference point for every later use-of-force debate. Each authorization for use of military force, including the 2001 AUMF, declares itself to be the ‘specific statutory authorization’ that Sec. 5(b) requires. Disputes usually turn on what counts as ‘hostilities’ and on whether a report was filed under Sec. 4(a)(1), which is what starts the clock.

title: War Powers Resolution
text:
Current status
In force. Every administration since Nixon has questioned the constitutionality of parts of it, and the 60-day clock has rarely been treated as binding. In 2026 House members introduced resolutions under it concerning U.S. military action in Venezuela and against Iran; their outcomes are not recorded here. Check current status.

title: Uniform Code of Military Justice
text:
In force Pub. L. 81-506 64 Stat. 107 10 U.S.C. 801-946a
The criminal code and court system of the U.S. armed forces. It replaced the separate Army and Navy disciplinary codes with one law for all services, defining military offenses, the types of courts-martial, the rights of the accused, and civilian appellate review.

title: Uniform Code of Military Justice
text:
Key provisions

Art. 2: who is subject to the code, including, since 2006, civilians accompanying forces in a contingency operation.
Art. 15: nonjudicial punishment by commanders for minor offenses.
Arts. 16-20: summary, special, and general courts-martial.
Arts. 77-134: the punitive articles, including Art. 92 on failure to obey a lawful order and Art. 134, the general article.
Arts. 141-146: the Court of Appeals for the Armed Forces, a civilian court.

title: Uniform Code of Military Justice
text:
Why it matters
It is the enforcement mechanism behind civilian control and the law of war inside the force: the duty to obey applies to lawful orders only. The Supreme Court measured the first Guantanamo commissions against it in Hamdan v. Rumsfeld, which led to the Military Commissions Act. Nearly all changes to it now arrive through the annual NDAA.

title: Uniform Code of Military Justice
text:
Current status
In force. Heavily revised by the Military Justice Act of 2016 (FY2017 defense authorization) and by the FY2022 defense authorization, which moved prosecution decisions for sexual assault, murder, and other covered offenses from commanders to independent special trial counsel, effective December 2023.

title: Taiwan Relations Act
text:
In force Pub. L. 96-8 93 Stat. 14 22 U.S.C. 3301 et seq.
Passed after the United States recognized the People’s Republic of China and ended formal relations with Taipei. It preserves unofficial ties, commits the United States to supply defensive arms, and states U.S. concern about any coercive resolution of Taiwan’s status.

title: Taiwan Relations Act
text:
Key provisions

Sec. 2: any non-peaceful effort to determine Taiwan’s future is a threat to peace and of grave concern to the United States.
Sec. 3: the United States will make available defensive arms, with the President and Congress determining what is needed.
Requires the United States to maintain the capacity to resist force or coercion against Taiwan.
Established the American Institute in Taiwan to conduct unofficial relations.

title: Taiwan Relations Act
text:

Congress wrote it to be firmer than the administration’s draft, and it is the statutory half of ‘strategic ambiguity’: it promises capacity and arms, not intervention. Arms sales under it follow the Arms Export Control Act procedures, and recent financing and stockpile authorities came through the annual NDAA.

title: Title 50, U.S. Code: War and National Defense
text:
In force 50 U.S.C. 1 et seq.
The title of the U.S. Code that collects the laws on war powers, emergency powers, intelligence, and economic defense. Unlike Title 10 it has no single design; it is a shelf holding statutes passed over two centuries.

title: Title 50, U.S. Code: War and National Defense
text:
Key provisions

Wartime authorities: the Alien Enemies Act (sec. 21) and the Trading with the Enemy Act (sec. 4301).
War and emergency powers: the War Powers Resolution (sec. 1541), the National Emergencies Act (sec. 1601), and the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (sec. 1701).
Intelligence: the National Security Act (sec. 3001), covert action and oversight (secs. 3091-3093), the CIA Act (sec. 3501), and FISA (sec. 1801).
Economic defense: the Defense Production Act (sec. 4501), foreign investment review (sec. 4565), and export controls (sec. 4801).
Manpower: the Military Selective Service Act (sec. 3801).

title: Title 50, U.S. Code: War and National Defense
text:
Why it matters
‘Title 50’ is shorthand for intelligence authority, above all covert action under a presidential finding, in contrast to military authority under Title 10. The shorthand understates the title: it also holds the main checks on presidential war and emergency power. The core of its intelligence chapters is the National Security Act.

title: Title 50, U.S. Code: War and National Defense
text:
Current status
In force. It is not positive law: it is an editorial compilation of separate statutes, so the underlying acts control. Many sections were renumbered in 2013 and the former appendix was folded into the main title in 2015.

title: About this wiki
text:
The wiki covers the federal statutes that most shape U.S. national security policy, in four core areas, plus a fifth group of foreign policy laws they connect to:

War powers and use of force
Intelligence and surveillance
Foreign aid, fragility, and sanctions
Defense organization and arms transfers
Related foreign policy legislation

A sixth group, constitutional and code foundations, holds what the rest is built on: the Constitution’s war and foreign affairs clauses, the founding-era statutes, the laws that created the National Guard, and overview pages for Titles 10, 22, 32, and 50 of the U.S. Code. Each title page lists every statute in the wiki codified in that title.
A few entries are single U.S. Code provisions, such as 10 U.S.C. 127e, where the provision matters more than the act that carried it. The Title 10 and Title 50 page explains the divide between military and intelligence authorities and lists the statutes in each title.
Apart from the Constitution page, it covers statutes only. Treaties, executive orders, court decisions, and regulations appear where they explain a statute, but they do not have their own pages.

text:
Member lens
This copy of the wiki is tailored to one member of Congress. The Member lens page maps that member’s committee seats, legislative record, and district interests onto the statutes. It is an independent reference built from public sources, it is not affiliated with or endorsed by the member’s office, and it describes the record without taking a position on it.

title: About this wiki
text:
Reading a statute page
Each page has the same parts: a citation bar with the law’s status, a short summary, key provisions, why the law matters, its current status, its connections to other statutes, and source links.
Links between statutes in the text and in the Connections table are the wiki’s cross-references. The knowledge graph draws the same connections.

title: About this wiki
text:
Relationship types
Connections are directional and use a fixed vocabulary.







Relationship
Meaning




amends
The first statute changed the text of the second.


repeals
The first statute repealed the second, in whole or in part.


succeeds
The first statute took over the role of the second.


relies on
The first statute operates through authority or machinery in the second.


constrains
The first statute limits how the second may be used.


enacted in
The first statute was passed as part of the second, usually a defense authorization.


related to
A thematic or historical link without a direct legal dependency.

title: About this wiki
text:
Status labels







Status
Meaning




In force
The statute is current law. It may have been amended.


Partly expired
Core provisions are current, but significant authorities have lapsed or depend on short extensions.


Lapsed
The central authority expired and had not been renewed at last review.


Repealed
Congress repealed the statute.


Superseded
A later statute replaced it.

title: About this wiki
text:
Accuracy and limits
The summaries were drafted with Claude, an AI model, and reviewed on November 10, 2026. Items that changed in 2025 and 2026 were checked against current reporting, and those sources are listed on the relevant pages. Citations and section numbers were written from reference knowledge and have not each been checked against the primary text.
Treat the wiki as a map for finding and relating statutes. Before citing a provision in your own work, confirm it in the primary source linked at the bottom of each page. Statutes with sunset clauses change fastest; the pages for Section 702, the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act, the Defense Production Act, the Iran Sanctions Act, and the annual defense authorization all carry a note to check current status.
Primary links are built from citations using fixed URL patterns. The GovInfo link service covers public laws from the 104th Congress (1995) onward and the Statutes at Large from volume 65 (1951) onward, so older laws link to the U.S. Code instead.
This is a reference tool and not legal advice.

title: About this wiki
text:
Adding or changing content
All content lives in data/. The pages in statutes/ are generated and should not be edited by hand.

Add or edit an entry in one of the files in data/statutes/. Copy an existing entry to get the fields right.
Add rows to data/edges.csv for its connections, using the relationship types above.
Run quarto preview. The build script checks the data and stops with a message if an ID, domain, status, or relationship is not recognized.

Each statute’s U.S. Code titles are read from its usc citation. To add a title that the citation does not show, list it under usc_titles, for example usc_titles: [10].
To link to another statute inside a summary, write its ID in double square brackets, for example [[fisa-1978]].

title: Arms Export Control Act
text:
In force Pub. L. 94-329 90 Stat. 729 22 U.S.C. 2751 et seq.
Governs U.S. arms exports. It sets the purposes for which American weapons may be sold, requires licenses for commercial sales, and gives Congress advance notice of major sales and a procedure to block them.

title: Arms Export Control Act
text:
Key provisions

Secs. 3 and 4: recipients may use U.S. arms only for self-defense, internal security, and similar purposes, and may not retransfer them without consent.
Sec. 36(b) and (c): notification to Congress of government and commercial sales above dollar thresholds, subject to a joint resolution of disapproval.
Sec. 36 emergency provision: the President may bypass the review period by declaring an emergency.
Sec. 38: licensing of commercial exports under the U.S. Munitions List and the International Traffic in Arms Regulations.
Sec. 40A: end-use monitoring.

title: Arms Export Control Act

Congress has never blocked a sale through a resolution of disapproval that survived a veto, so its influence runs through informal holds and conditions. title: U.S. Constitution: War and Foreign Affairs Powers
text:
In force
The Constitution divides national security powers between Congress and the President and leaves the boundary largely undefined. Every statute in this wiki is an exercise of, or an argument about, one of these clauses.

title: U.S. Constitution: War and Foreign Affairs Powers
text:
Key provisions

Art. I, Sec. 8, cl. 11: Congress declares war and grants letters of marque and reprisal.
Art. I, Sec. 8, cls. 12-14: Congress raises and supports armies (with appropriations limited to two years), maintains a navy, and makes rules for the armed forces.
Art. I, Sec. 8, cls. 15-16: Congress provides for calling forth and organizing the militia.
Art. I, Sec. 8, cl. 18 and Sec. 9, cl. 7: the necessary and proper power and the requirement that money be spent only under appropriations.
Art. II, Sec. 2: the President is commander in chief, makes treaties with the consent of two thirds of the Senate, and appoints ambassadors and officers.
Art. II, Sec. 3 and Art. IV, Sec. 4: the duty to see the laws faithfully executed, and the guarantee to protect states against invasion and domestic violence.

title: U.S. Constitution: War and Foreign Affairs Powers
text:
Why it matters
The standard framework for disputes is Justice Jackson’s concurrence in Youngstown Sheet and Tube Co. v. Sawyer (1952): presidential power is strongest when Congress has authorized the action and weakest when Congress has forbidden it. That is why framework statutes such as the War Powers Resolution and the National Emergencies Act matter even when they are not enforced in court. The militia clauses are the source of the Militia Acts of 1792 and, through them, the Insurrection Act.

title: U.S. Constitution: War and Foreign Affairs Powers

title: Defense Production Act of 1950
text:

Title III: loans, loan guarantees, purchase commitments, and direct investment to expand domestic production.

‘National defense’ is defined broadly to include energy, critical infrastructure, and emergency preparedness.

title: Foreign Assistance Act of 1961
text:
In force Pub. L. 87-195 75 Stat. 424 22 U.S.C. 2151 et seq.
The basic law of U.S. foreign aid. It separated economic from military assistance, set the purposes and conditions of each, and led President Kennedy to create the U.S. Agency for International Development by executive order two months later.

title: Foreign Assistance Act of 1961
text:
Key provisions

Part I: development assistance, including health, education, democracy, and disaster relief authorities.
Part II: security assistance, including the Economic Support Fund, military education and training, peacekeeping, and Section 506 drawdown authority.
Secs. 116 and 502B: human rights conditions on economic and security assistance.
Sec. 620 and following: country and conduct restrictions, including the Cuba embargo authority in Sec. 620(a).
Sec. 634A: advance notice to Congress before funds are reprogrammed.

title: Foreign Assistance Act of 1961
text:
Why it matters
Most later aid and security assistance law is written as an amendment or companion to this act: the Leahy Laws, the Symington-Glenn Amendments, the Hughes-Ryan Amendment, the Global Fragility Act, and the military sales side that became the Arms Export Control Act. Its age and accumulated amendments are a common argument for rewriting it.

title: Foreign Assistance Act of 1961
text:
Current status
In force. It has not had a comprehensive reauthorization since 1985, so foreign aid policy is mostly set through annual appropriations acts.

text:

title: National Defense Act of 1916
text:
Superseded Pub. L. 64-85 39 Stat. 166 10 U.S.C. 10101 et seq.
The first comprehensive statute organizing U.S. land forces. It defined the Army as the Regular Army, the National Guard, and a federal reserve, and it let the President draft the Guard into federal service for use overseas.

title: National Defense Act of 1916
text:
Key provisions

Defined the components of the Army and expanded its authorized strength.
Guard members took a dual oath to state and nation and could be drafted into federal service in war.
Created the Reserve Officers’ Training Corps and an organized reserve.
Gave the President authority to place obligatory orders with industry in war, an early precedent for defense production powers.

title: National Defense Act of 1916
text:
Why it matters
It set the three-component structure the Army still has. The 1933 amendments completed the design by making Guard members simultaneously members of a federal reserve component, which is what today’s mobilization authorities operate on. Its industrial mobilization section anticipates the Defense Production Act.

title: National Defense Act of 1916
text:
Current status

title: National Emergencies Act
text:
In force Pub. L. 94-412 90 Stat. 1255 50 U.S.C. 1601-1651
Ended the open-ended emergencies that had accumulated since the 1930s and set procedures for declaring, renewing, and terminating national emergencies. A declaration unlocks more than a hundred standby statutory powers, but the President must specify which ones are being used.

title: National Emergencies Act
text:
Key provisions

Title I: terminated powers exercised under emergencies in effect in 1976.
Sec. 201: the President declares an emergency by proclamation published in the Federal Register.
Sec. 202: emergencies lapse after one year unless renewed; Congress may terminate by joint resolution (changed from concurrent resolution in 1985) and is directed to consider termination every six months.
Sec. 301: the President must name the statutory authorities being invoked.
Title IV: accounting and reporting requirements.

title: National Emergencies Act
text:
Why it matters
It is the procedural gateway for IEEPA, so nearly every U.S. economic sanctions program rests on a declaration made under it. Because termination now requires a joint resolution that the President can veto, critics argue the check Congress intended in 1976 is much weaker in practice.

title: National Emergencies Act
text:
Current status
In force. Dozens of declared emergencies remain active, most of them sanctions programs that are renewed every year.

title: National Security Act of 1947
text:
In force Pub. L. 80-253 61 Stat. 495 50 U.S.C. 3001 et seq.
The founding charter of the modern national security system. It created the National Security Council and the Central Intelligence Agency, established a separate Air Force, and placed the military departments under a single Secretary of Defense.

title: National Security Act of 1947
text:
Key provisions

Title I: National Security Council and Central Intelligence Agency; since 2004 also the Director of National Intelligence.
Title II: the National Military Establishment, which 1949 amendments turned into the Department of Defense.
Title V (added 1980, expanded 1991): congressional oversight of intelligence, including covert action findings at 50 U.S.C. 3093.
Sec. 108 (50 U.S.C. 3043): the annual National Security Strategy report, added in 1986.

title: National Security Act of 1947
text:

title: National Security Act of 1947
text:
Current status

title: USA PATRIOT Act
text:
Partly expired Pub. L. 107-56 115 Stat. 272
An omnibus counterterrorism law passed six weeks after September 11. It widened surveillance and information-sharing authorities, expanded anti-money-laundering rules, and broadened terrorism offenses and immigration exclusions.

title: USA PATRIOT Act
text:
Key provisions

Sec. 215: orders for ‘any tangible things’ relevant to a terrorism or counterintelligence investigation.
Sec. 218: foreign intelligence need only be ‘a significant purpose’ of FISA surveillance, lowering the wall between intelligence and criminal investigators.
Sec. 505: broader use of national security letters.
Title III: anti-money-laundering measures, including Section 311 special measures against foreign jurisdictions and banks.
Sec. 805: expanded the definition of material support for terrorism.

title: USA PATRIOT Act
text:
Why it matters
It reshaped FISA and the material support offenses created by AEDPA. The bulk telephone metadata program later justified under Section 215 led directly to the USA FREEDOM Act.

title: USA PATRIOT Act
text:
Current status
Most of the act is permanent. Section 215 (business records) and section 206 (roving wiretaps), along with the lone wolf provision, expired on March 15, 2020 and have not been renewed.

title: Reserve and National Guard Mobilization Authorities
text:
In force Pub. L. 82-476 66 Stat. 481 10 U.S.C. 12301-12304b, 12406
The set of Title 10 provisions, descended from the Armed Forces Reserve Act of 1952 and earlier militia acts, that let the federal government order reserve forces and the National Guard to active duty. Each tier has its own trigger, size limit, and duration.

title: Reserve and National Guard Mobilization Authorities
text:
Key provisions

Sec. 12301(a): full mobilization in a war or national emergency declared by Congress, for the duration plus six months.
Sec. 12302: partial mobilization of up to 1,000,000 reservists for up to 24 months under a national emergency declared by the President.
Sec. 12304: presidential call-up of up to 200,000 reservists for up to 365 days without a declared emergency.
Secs. 12304a and 12304b: call-ups for disaster response and for preplanned missions supporting combatant commands.
Sec. 12406: the President may call the National Guard into federal service in case of invasion, rebellion, or inability to execute the laws with the regular forces.
By contrast, Guard members serving under Title 32 remain under state command while federally funded.

title: Reserve and National Guard Mobilization Authorities
text:
Why it matters
Which authority is used decides who commands the troops and what they may do: Guard members federalized under Title 10 fall under the Posse Comitatus Act, while those in state or Title 32 status do not. Section 12406 is an alternative route to the Insurrection Act, and Section 12302 depends on an emergency declared under the National Emergencies Act.

title: Reserve and National Guard Mobilization Authorities
text:
Current status
In force. On December 23, 2025 the Supreme Court, in Trump v. Illinois, left in place an order blocking a National Guard federalization under Section 12406(3), reasoning that ‘regular forces’ in that section likely means the regular military. The administration then ended its deployments under that section. The ruling came on an emergency application and litigation may continue. Check current status.

Lets the Secretary of Defense fund foreign forces, irregular forces, groups, or individuals who support or facilitate ongoing U.S. special operations against terrorism. These are surrogate forces working to U.S. objectives, as distinct from partner forces being built up for their own missions.

title: Emergency Military Construction Authority (10 U.S.C. 2808)
text:
In force Pub. L. 97-214 96 Stat. 153 10 U.S.C. 2808
One of the standby powers unlocked by a national emergency. When a declared war or emergency requires use of the armed forces, the Secretary of Defense may build military construction projects that Congress never authorized, using unspent military construction funds.

title: Emergency Military Construction Authority (10 U.S.C. 2808)
text:
Key provisions

Trigger: a declaration of war, or a national emergency declared by the President that requires use of the armed forces.
Projects must be necessary to support that use of the armed forces.
Funding comes from military construction money already appropriated and not yet obligated.
Congress must be notified of each decision and its cost.

title: Emergency Military Construction Authority (10 U.S.C. 2808)
text:
Why it matters
Used quietly for overseas projects after 2001, it became prominent in 2019 when 3.6 billion dollars was moved from other projects to border barriers. It is the standard worked example of how the National Emergencies Act converts a proclamation into spending power, and the later cap came through the annual NDAA.

title: Emergency Military Construction Authority (10 U.S.C. 2808)
text:
Current status
In force. The FY2021 defense authorization capped its use at 500 million dollars per emergency, and 100 million for projects inside the United States.

title: Military Cyber Operations Authority (10 U.S.C. 394-395)
text:

title: Military Selective Service Act
text:
Partly expired Pub. L. 80-759 62 Stat. 604 50 U.S.C. 3801 et seq.

title: Military Selective Service Act
text:
Key provisions

Registration of male citizens and most male residents aged 18 through 25.
Classification, deferment, and conscientious objector provisions.

title: Title 10, U.S. Code: Armed Forces
text:
In force Pub. L. 84-1028 70A Stat. 1 10 U.S.C. 101 et seq.
The title of the U.S. Code that governs the armed forces: their organization, command, personnel, training, procurement, and reserve components. Congress enacted it as positive law in 1956, so its text is itself the law and not just evidence of it.

title: Title 10, U.S. Code: Armed Forces
text:
Key provisions

Subtitle A, General Military Law: the Department of Defense, the Joint Chiefs and combatant commands, personnel, the Uniform Code of Military Justice, training, and acquisition.
Subtitle B: Army. Subtitle C: Navy and Marine Corps. Subtitle D: Air Force and Space Force.
Subtitle E: Reserve Components, including the mobilization authorities.

title: Title 10, U.S. Code: Armed Forces

‘Title 10’ is shorthand for military authority exercised through the chain of command, as opposed to intelligence authority under Title 50, diplomatic and assistance authority under Title 22, or National Guard service under Title 32. Its structure was set by the National Security Act and its amendments, and nearly all changes now come through the annual NDAA.

text:
In force Pub. L. 84-1028 70A Stat. 596 32 U.S.C. 101 et seq.
The title of the U.S. Code for the National Guard when it is not in federal service. It governs organization, federal funding, and training of the Guard while it remains under the command of state governors.

title: Title 32, U.S. Code: National Guard
text:
Key provisions

Federal recognition, organization, and equipment standards for the Guard.

title: Title 32, U.S. Code: National Guard
text:

‘Title 32 status’ is the middle position between purely state service and federal service under Title 10: federal money and missions, state command. Because troops in that status are not federal forces, the Posse Comitatus Act does not apply to them, which is why the choice of status under the mobilization authorities is often the decisive legal question in domestic deployments. Its roots are in the Militia Act of 1903.

title: Gulf of Tonkin Resolution
text:
Repealed Pub. L. 88-408 78 Stat. 384
A joint resolution approving ‘all necessary measures’ by the President to repel attacks on U.S. forces and prevent further aggression in Southeast Asia. It became the legal foundation for the escalation of the Vietnam War.

title: Gulf of Tonkin Resolution
text:
Key provisions

Approved and supported the President’s determination to take all necessary measures to repel armed attack and prevent further aggression.
Authorized force to assist any member or protocol state of the Southeast Asia Collective Defense Treaty that requested help.
Would expire when the President determined peace was secured, or earlier by concurrent resolution of Congress.

title: Gulf of Tonkin Resolution

title: Trading with the Enemy Act of 1917
text:
In force Pub. L. 65-91 40 Stat. 411 50 U.S.C. 4301-4341
A First World War statute giving the President sweeping control over trade and property involving enemy countries and nationals. Between 1933 and 1977 its Section 5(b) also applied in declared peacetime emergencies and became the all-purpose economic sanctions authority.

title: Trading with the Enemy Act of 1917
text:
Key provisions

Sec. 5(b): power to regulate or prohibit transactions in foreign exchange and property in which a foreign country or national has an interest.
Authority to seize and vest enemy property.
1977 amendment: confined Sec. 5(b) to wartime while allowing existing programs to be extended one year at a time.

title: Trading with the Enemy Act of 1917
text:

title: United Nations Participation Act of 1945
text:
In force Pub. L. 79-264 59 Stat. 619 22 U.S.C. 287-287e
Governs U.S. participation in the United Nations: how representatives are appointed, how the United States carries out Security Council decisions, and the terms on which U.S. forces may be made available to the Council.

title: United Nations Participation Act of 1945
text:
Key provisions

Sec. 5 (22 U.S.C. 287c): the President may implement Security Council measures not involving armed force, such as sanctions, with criminal penalties for violations.

Sec. 7 (added 1949): allows detail of up to 1,000 personnel to U.N. activities in noncombatant roles.
